question_text: In functional programming, how does Currying differ from Partial Application?

options.text: Currying translates a function of N arguments into a chain of N single-argument functions; Partial Application binds a fixed subset of arguments returning a function of lower arity
Currying is asynchronous; Partial Application is synchronous
Partial application requires macros; currying is native to all languages
They are identical mathematical operations with differing syntax

answer_explanation: Currying decomposes `f(a, b, c)` strictly into `f(a)(b)(c)`. Partial application takes `f(a, b, c)` and fixes `a` to return `g(b, c)`.
reference_solution: Correct Choice: A. Rationale: Currying decomposes `f(a, b, c)` strictly into `f(a)(b)(c)`. Partial application takes `f(a, b, c)` and fixes `a` to return `g(b, c)`.
